The signed December 27 ministerial order A/2025/1397/MATD/CAB/SGG was freshly recovered as a two-page scan hosted by Le Lynx and visually inspected. Article 2 uses the same Saturday-midnight to Sunday-midnight wording as the embassy report; air closure is separately 05:00–20:00 Sunday. Domestic vehicle restrictions and their exceptions remain separate.

An independent LégisGuinée transcription describes different all-mode hours and article numbering; its underlying alleged Journal officiel page was not recovered. No evidence establishes that text as an amendment, so it does not replace the inspected signed order. Actual gate reopening and exact operational duration remain unobserved.

Source provenance: the embassy-hosted article explicitly credits Bhoye Barry for Guinee7.com. It is a news republication, not an independent government statement; the signed ministerial scan is the primary policy evidence.

phases.Qualification:
March 17 selective restrictions and April 30 customs status are directly supported. The March 16, 2022 cabinet statement expressly describes land, air and sea entry subject to negative PCR or antigen tests, and exits subject to destination-country requirements. It no longer describes eligibility as limited to indispensable journeys. We therefore infer an earlier ended-by bound for the essential-only restriction from this general traveller regime. The statement does not explicitly name a repeal clause or identify the first ordinary passenger crossing.

June 16, 2022 removes later testing/document requirements; it should not prolong the earlier essential-travel closure interval. Neither observation proves continuous enforcement since March 2020. Cargo and indispensable-travel exceptions, and independent neighbouring-country restrictions, remain separate.

phases.Qualification:
NAN and contemporary Nigerian local reporting quote the customs controller describing the Nigerian reopening decision and actual February 9, 2026 truck clearance; NAN also quotes a Niger representative welcoming that decision. Anadolu independently attributes the months-long measure to Nigeria. This supports recording Nigerian involvement, rather than treating it as solely Niger-imposed.

Banouto attributes the preceding blockage to Niger while describing the Nigerian reopening. Its disagreement remains visible; separate concurrent measures may have been conflated. No original closure order or precise onset was recovered. Officials’ descriptions of months of disruption establish a >24-hour restriction, but neither the three-month shorthand nor broad seven-year retrospective accounts establish an exact continuous interval. The 2019 trade regime, 2022 Kamba permission and direct Benin–Niger frontier restriction remain separate.
